title: Summarizing Known Attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS)
summary: This informational document summarizes several serious attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS), including attacks on commonly used ciphers and modes of operation. It aims to motivate generic and protocol-specific recommendations for using TLS and DTLS safely.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gathers serious attacks known against TLS and DTLS when it was written. It explains what the attacks target and notes some ways to reduce the risks.

subtitle: A snapshot of attacks on TLS and DTLS that motivated safer-use recommendations.

tldr.problem: Several serious attacks affected TLS, including weaknesses in widely used ciphers, modes, and implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes attacks on downgrade handling, CBC, RC4, compression, keys, handshakes, virtual hosts, and implementations, with mitigations where the text identifies them.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC is a snapshot of knowledge at publication, not an exhaustive survey. It says new attacks may be discovered.

facts.label: DTLS 1.0 comparison
facts.value: Equivalent to TLS 1.1 for these attacks; RC4 is disallowed

today: RFC 7457 is an Informational RFC published in February 2015. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC describes its contents as a snapshot at that time.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7457 summarizes attacks that motivated recommendations for using Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS). The authors emphasize that the list is not an extensive survey and reflects knowledge at the time of writing.

Unless the DTLS section says otherwise, the attacks discussed also apply to DTLS. The document describes attacks informationally and does not itself add security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: This document records attacks known when it was published. It is a snapshot, so it cannot cover attacks discovered later.

sections.title: Downgrades, Padding, Ciphers, and Compression
sections.content:
SSL stripping and STARTTLS downgrade attacks try to prevent a connection from upgrading to TLS; HSTS is noted as a mitigation for web traffic. BEAST targets the predictable initialization vector in TLS 1.0 CBC. Lucky Thirteen exploits a timing difference in padding checks, while POODLE targets SSL 3.0 and has no known mitigation in the RFC.

The RFC says RC4 keystream biases can expose repeated plaintexts. CRIME targets TLS compression, while TIME and BREACH exploit HTTP compression; disabling TLS compression mitigates TIME, but BREACH needs application-level mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: Some attacks prevent encryption from starting, while others exploit details of encryption or compression. The RFC gives specific mitigations for some attacks and says no TLS-level fix was known for others.

sections.title: Certificates, Keys, and Handshakes
sections.content:
The RFC describes attacks involving RSA certificates, certificate validation, private-key theft, and Diffie-Hellman parameters. It notes that stolen private keys can expose sessions using most non-Diffie-Hellman cipher suites, while forward-secrecy cipher suites reduce that risk for passive attackers.

Other attacks exploit renegotiation or cause two TLS connections to share keying material. The RFC points to the renegotiation indication extension in RFC 5746 as the resolution for the renegotiation attack it discusses.
sections.plainLanguage: Weak certificate checks or stolen keys can undermine protected connections. Some attacks target how handshakes establish or reuse security information.

sections.title: Virtual Hosts, Denial of Service, and Implementations
sections.content:
The RFC describes virtual-host confusion involving SSLv3 fallback and server session-cache handling. It also notes that a client can make a server perform much more computational work than the client performs.

Implementation problems include omitting certificate checks, failing to match the server name to the certificate, and incorrect chain validation. Heartbleed is cited as a bounds-checking coding error discovered in April 2014; user behavior around invalid-certificate warnings is also discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: A secure protocol can still be undermined by software errors or unsafe certificate handling. People who routinely accept certificate warnings can also weaken protection.

sections.title: How the Findings Apply to DTLS
sections.content:
DTLS adapts TLS for UDP. For the attacks in this RFC, DTLS 1.0 is equivalent to TLS 1.1 except that RC4 is disallowed in DTLS; DTLS 1.2 is equivalent to TLS 1.2.

The RFC itself is informational and says it has no security implications. Its companion documents, especially the secure-use recommendations cited by the RFC, address recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS carries TLS-like security over datagrams. Most attacks in this RFC also apply to it, with the stated RC4 exception for DTLS 1.0.
